1. Introduction
Line Intensity Mapping (LIM) is an observational technique
designed to measure the integrated spectral line emission
from all galaxies in a population, while generating a three-
dimensional fluctuation map of a given spectral line with in-
tentionally broadened spatial resolution. Specifically, this tech-
nique is sensitive to the integrated emission from even the
faintest end of the luminosity function, and is thus a pos-
sible solution to the completeness problem in (particularly
high-redshift) galaxy surveys. For a review, see Kovetz et al.
(2019). LIM is still an emerging field – no experiment has
yet made a confirmed auto-correlation detection of their tar-
get emission line (e.g., Staniszewski et al. 2014; Keating et al.
2015; Keating et al. 2020; Cleary et al. 2022; Fasano et al. 2022;
CCAT-Prime Collaboration et al. 2023; Paul et al. 2023), due to
the faintness of the target signal, the need for exquisite control of
instrumental systematic errors and, in some cases, the presence
of interloper spectral line emission.
⋆e-mail: ddunne@astro.caltech.edu
Because of these difficulties, analysis techniques that com-
bine LIM data with external tracers of the matter density (such as
other intensity mapping experiments or more traditional galaxy
surveys) will be an extremely valuable way of validating poten-
tial auto-correlation detections as the field matures. These joint
analyses upweight regions of the LIM map that are most likely
to contain signal and so can mitigate the effects of instrumental
and astrophysical systematic error, as these should primarily be
unique to one of the two tracers included in the analysis.
The most commonly-studied technique for combining
intensity mapping data with a galaxy survey is a full
three-dimensional cross-correlation (e.g., Pullen et al. 2013;
Chung et al. 2019; Keenan et al. 2022; Breysse & Alexandroff
2019), as this allows for study of the interaction between the
two tracers as a function of spatial scale. However, this is sen-
sitive to any existing angular structure in either survey strategy,
and suffers from complicated mode-mixing effects when angular
structure in the two experiments correlate. These problems are
tractable, but complex to manage, particularly in the early stages
of an experiment. Because of this, several LIM experiments

are turning towards an analysis that is simpler conceptually –
a three-dimensional stack, or co-addition, of the LIM data on
the positions of objects in the galaxy survey (e.g. Keenan et al.
2022; Dunne et al. 2024). Functionally, this is equivalent to the
zero-lag region of the two-point correlation function, or a real-
space version of a cross-correlation on the smallest spatial scale.
Although the stack is conceptually simple, it is also more
sensitive to astrophysical effects and it is generally unclear in
practice how these will affect its output. Previous work has
shown that, for example, astrophysical line broadening has
a dampening effect on cross-correlations that is worst in the
highest-k bin (e.g. Chung et al. 2021). These effects need to be
explored in detail with simulations. Therefore, in this work, we
devise a simple yet robust simulation pipeline that can gener-
ate a realistic population of multiple astrophysical tracers, as
well as parameterize the interaction between the two. Using this
pipeline, we aim to answer the following questions:
1. What experimental design (of both the LIM and catalogue
experiment) is optimal for a stacking analysis?
2. Where does the signal in a stacking analysis originate?
3. What can the stack tell us about the properties of the galaxies
contributing to the signal?
We structure the work as follows: in §2, we introduce the
joint simulation pipeline, which is an extension to the existing
limlam_mocker1 simulation pipeline. We briefly summarize the
stacking methodology in §3, and attempt to parameterize the
stack analytically. We then test the effects of various instrumen-
tal and astrophysical parameters on the outcome of the stacking
analysis in §4. In §5, we discuss the implications of these results.
We assume base-10 logarithms unless otherwise stated, and
where necessary we take a ΛCDM cosmology with Ωm = 0.286,
ΩΛ = 0.714, Ωb = 0.047, and H0 = 100hkm s−1 Mpc−1 with
h = 0.7. This matches the choice of parameters used in the peak-
patch simulations in §2 and is based on the nine-year WMAP re-
sults (Hinshaw et al. 2013). All cosmological distances are pre-
sented as comoving quantities.
2. Simulated Multi-Tracer Observations
Because LIM targets cosmological scales but is also sensitive
to variations in spectral-line emission at the level of an individ-
ual dark matter (DM) halo, observational LIM data are difficult
to simulate. For joint analyses such as the stack being explored
in this work, we are additionally including a second spectral-
line tracer, and thus need to realistically simulate the distribu-
tion across halo masses of both tracers, as well as the interaction
between the tracers at the individual halo level.
For this work, we follow previous efforts to simulate LIM
data using the limlam_mocker pipeline, adding the capability to
generate a galaxy catalogue using a different spectral-line tracer.
The overall flow of the pipeline is outlined in Figure 1, and is
as follows: we begin with a dark matter (DM) halo catalogue
generated from peak-patch N-body simulations (§2.1). We then
assign to each halo simulated luminosities corresponding to each
of two different emission lines calculated based on the halo’s
dark matter (DM) mass – one line associated with the LIM map
(§2.2) and one associated with the galaxy catalogue (§2.3). We
add scatter to each luminosity value, correlated between the two
tracers on a per-halo basis (§2.4). We then generate a synthetic
line intensity map (§2.5) and a synthetic galaxy catalogue (§2.6).

The outputs of the simulation pipeline are multi-survey and

instrumental or astrophysical parameters, such as spectral line
broadening, interloper emission in the LIM map, and redshift
uncertainties in the galaxy catalogue. Although the treatment of
these astrophysical and instrumental parameters is basic, we can
vary the prescription used for any of the steps in this process,
in order to explore the importance of each step to the stacking
analysis.

Each DM halo is assigned a set of spectral lines, each with a
redshift and a luminosity, which are used to generate the LIM
and galaxy surveys. The LIM data cube is generated by summing

Each line's contribution is weighted by the halo's LCO and LLyα

3.1. LIM Line Generation
The LIM data cube is generated by summing over all halos, each
halo contributing a line emission at their respective rest wavelength.
The line flux at each wavelength is given by:
Fλ = F0 × (1 + z) × LCO(Mh) × δ(λ − λ_obs(λ_rest, z))
(8)
where F0 is a scaling factor, z is the redshift, and δ is the
Dirac delta function. We have to account for the fact that the
luminosity of the line is proportional to the number of clouds
in the halo, and that the flux is proportional to the integrated
luminosity of the clouds along the line of sight. The factor F0
is determined by the requirement that the integrated flux over all
wavelengths matches the observed total luminosity of the halo.
This is achieved by setting F0 = LCO(Mh) × f0, where f0 is a
constant scaling factor that we can choose to normalize the overall
flux.

3.2. Lyα Line Generation
The Lyα line generation is similar, but uses the Lyα luminosity
LLyα(Mh) instead of LCO. The line flux is:
Fλ = F0 × (1 + z) × LLyα(Mh) × δ(λ − λ_obs(λ_rest, z))
(9)
where F0 is the same as in equation (8).

The LIM data cube is observed in a three-dimensional grid of
pixels, each with a redshift and spatial position. The spatial
density of the halos determines the number of lines contributing
to each pixel. The redshift distribution of the halos determines
the number of lines at each wavelength. The observed flux in each
pixel is the sum of the fluxes from all lines in that pixel.

Similarly, the Lyα line catalogue is generated by assigning each
halo a position in the sky, and a redshift, and then creating a
synthetic galaxy catalogue where each galaxy is a point source
at the position of the DM halo, with a flux determined by the
Lyα luminosity of the halo.

of each halo. The standard deviation of this Gaussian is a
parameter of the simulation, and can vary between the two surveys.

For the example case we are exploring – a stack on a CO LIM
map using a Lyα catalogue – an empirically-motivated choice
of ρ is difficult owing to the lack of available simultaneous ob-
servations of CO and Lyα in galaxies (especially at higher red-
shifts). For the purposes of this work, we look at the relationship
between CO and Lyα via galaxy metallicity. Davis et al. (2023)
found the LAEs catalogued by HETDEX to be primarily com-
prised of galaxies with young, metal-poor stellar populations
(Z ∼0.2 −0.3 Z⊙). This agrees with other surveys of (especially
lower-luminosity) LAEs (e.g. Sobral et al. 2018; Matthee et al.
2021). CO emission, however, is typically suppressed in actively
star-forming low-metallicity galaxies (Bolatto et al. 2013). We
can thus expect at least a slight anti-correlation between emis-
sion in the two lines on an individual galaxy level, no matter how
their overall populations correlate with DM halo mass. With this
as justification, we default to a value of ρ = −0.5 for the pur-
poses of this paper. We note that, particularly for our default CO
and Lyα configuration, this choice does not significantly affect
our results – we explore the effects of varying ρ in §4.4.3.

To mimic line foregrounds or backgrounds, we add sim-

than simulating the interloper emission from scratch. This is an
inaccurate representation of the large-scale structure of the inter-
loper emission, but the stack is not very sensitive to large-scale
structure, so this should not affect our results. The transforma-
tion is done using one of 11 rotations or reflections:
1. One of three rotations (by 90◦, 180◦, or 270◦) in the spatial
axes
2. One of two reflections (in either the RA or Dec axis)
3. A reflection across the frequency axis
4. A reflection across the frequency axis, combined with any of
the spatial rotations or reflections.
We then scale the brightness of this transformed map to match
the expected luminosity of foreground lines compared to CO.
A factor of 10 roughly corresponds to the difference between
CO(1–0) at cosmic noon and the next most significant source
of emission in our frequency range: CO(2-1) at 6 < z < 8,
which is expected to be roughly an order of magnitude fainter
(Chung et al. 2024b). We then add the interloper map to the map
of simulated CO emission.
Finally, we subtract from the map a mean across the spatial
dimensions in each spectral channel and across the spectral axis
in each spaxel. This emulates the high-pass spatial and spectral
filters in the actual COMAP data pipeline, which reject contin-
uum emission almost entirely (Lunde et al. 2024). For this rea-
son, we ignore continuum emission when inserting an interloper
signal.
2.6. Simulated Galaxy catalogue
We generate a galaxy catalogue from the set of simulated halos
simply by logging the three-dimensional positions (and, option-
ally, luminosities) of some subset of the DM halos. This subset
is generated by first cutting on luminosity, including only halos
above a certain tracer luminosity LLyα,cut, in order to simulate ob-
servational completeness. We note that this should more properly
be a cut in flux, as flux (rather than luminosity) is the quantity
observed by the telescope. The conversion between flux and lu-
minosity is redshift-dependent, so the completeness limit should
also be redshift dependent. However, the effect of this change on
the returned number counts of catalogued galaxies even at the
edges of the COMAP redshift range is small (roughly 10%). Ad-
ditionally, most spectrographs have sensitivities which vary with
wavelength, so the limiting catalogue luminosity will in practice
be a function of redshift due to instrumental effects. Here, how-
ever, we treat it as constant.
We then pick Nobj halos with LLyα > LLyα,cut randomly,
weighting linearly by LLyα as brighter objects are more likely
to be detected. Nobj is set by the observational parameters of the
galaxy survey being approximated. In practice, this selection will
be subject to the observing pattern of the galaxy survey used, but
the stack is not sensitive to large scales and thus large-scale spa-
tial correlations here should not be important. Figure 2 shows an
example simulation of the Lyα population as well as the halos
which are selected by the detectability cuts to be included in the
mock catalogue.

present between the two tracers, but assume that these will be
well-characterized and thus easily accounted for.
